s0000 00:00:01 S1: ¶|·        Let's start with the set piece, because that is where your teams are known.
s0001 00:00:11 S2: ¶|         The scrum is a contest of angles before it is a contest of strength.
s0002 00:00:20 S2:            If the tight head's shoulder is above his hip the pressure goes nowhere.
s0003 00:00:29 S2:   ·        We film every scrum from behind the posts so the players see their own body height.
s0004 00:00:41 S1: ¶|·        How much of that is coachable and how much is simply size?
s0005 00:00:49 S2: ¶|         Size buys you a margin, but technique is what survives eighty minutes.
s0006 00:00:58 S2:            Our lightest prop last season won more penalties than anyone in the league.
s0007 00:01:07 S2:   ·        He did it by getting his bind earlier than the man opposite him.
s0008 00:01:16 S1: ¶|·        And the line-out, is that a different skill entirely?
s0009 00:01:23 S2: ¶|         The line-out is a timing problem dressed up as a jumping problem.
s0010 00:01:32 S2:            The lifters have to be moving before the hooker's hands leave the ball.
s0011 00:01:41 S2:   ·        We drill the call to the throw in under two seconds, every session.
s0012 00:01:50 S1: ¶|·        Do you change the calls much during a match?
s0013 00:01:57 S2: ¶|         We carry four and we use two, because a caller who is thinking is a caller who is late.
s0014 00:02:09 S2:            The opposition scout our first six line-outs and we know that they do.
s0015 00:02:18 S2:   ·        So the sixth one is usually the one we have been saving.
s0016 00:02:27 S1: ¶|·        What about the breakdown, which everyone says is where matches are won?
s0017 00:02:36 S2: ¶|         The breakdown rewards whoever arrives with their feet already set.
s0018 00:02:44 S2:            A player who arrives fast and off balance gives away the penalty every time.
s0019 00:02:53 S2:   ·        We coach the last three steps before the ruck, not the sprint into it.
s0020 00:03:03 S1: ¶|·        Is that why your penalty count dropped so sharply last year?
s0021 00:03:12 S2: ¶|         Partly, and partly because we stopped asking the flankers to compete on every ball.
s0022 00:03:22 S2:            Choosing three rucks a half to attack is worth more than contesting thirty.
s0023 00:03:31 S2:   ·        The referee starts to trust a pack that is not always on the edge.
s0024 00:03:41 S1: ¶|·        How do you decide which three?
s0025 00:03:46 S2: ¶|         We look for the ruck after a big carry, when their support is still getting up.
s0026 00:03:56 S2:            That is the moment the ball is slowest and the guard is thinnest.
s0027 00:04:05 S2:   ·        Everything else we leave alone and get back into the defensive line.
s0028 00:04:14 S1: ¶|·        Does any of this change on a wet night in February?
s0029 00:04:22 S2: ¶|         The weather changes the reward, not the method.
s0030 00:04:28 S2:            In the wet the scrum is worth more because the backs will not run from deep.
s0031 00:04:39 S2:   ·        So we shorten the game and make them play in front of their own posts.
s0032 00:04:49 S1: ¶|·        What do you look for when you recruit a young forward?
s0033 00:04:57 S2: ¶|         Work rate first, because you cannot teach a man to want the next collision.
s0034 00:05:07 S2:            Then neck and shoulder strength, because that part takes the longest to build.
s0035 00:05:16 S2:   ·        Skills we can add, and we can add them quickly at that age.

s0037 00:05:33 S2: ¶|         Packs that push straight when they should be pushing across.
s0038 00:05:41 S2:            A straight shove against a good front row is a shove into a wall.
s0039 00:05:50 S2:   ·        The angle is free and almost nobody takes it.
s0040 00:05:58 S1: ¶|·        I want to change subject completely, because you also write about money.
s0041 00:06:07 S2: ¶|         Compound interest is the one idea in finance that everybody agrees on.
s0042 00:06:15 S2:            It works because the return itself starts earning a return of its own.
s0043 00:06:24 S2:   ·        The first ten years look disappointing and the last ten look like magic.
s0044 00:06:34 S1: ¶|·        Why do people give up during the disappointing part?
s0045 00:06:41 S2: ¶|         Because the curve is almost flat there, and a flat curve feels like failure.
s0046 00:06:51 S2:            A pound saved in the first year is worth many pounds saved in the twentieth.
s0047 00:07:01 S2:   ·        But it does not feel that way while you are saving it.
s0048 00:07:09 S1: ¶|·        What do you tell someone starting at forty rather than at twenty?

s0050 00:07:26 S2:            They have to save a larger share and they have to leave it alone for longer.

s0053 00:07:51 S2: ¶|         I mean anything at all that promises to shorten the wait.
s0054 00:07:58 S2:            The wait is the product, and the return is what you are paid for enduring it.
s0055 00:08:09 S2:   ·        Every scheme that removes the wait puts something worse in its place.
s0056 00:08:18 S1: ¶|·        So a broad index fund and nothing else?
s0057 00:08:24 S2: ¶|         For almost everybody, a broad index fund at a low fee is the whole answer.
s0058 00:08:34 S2:            The fee matters more than people believe, because the fee compounds as well.
s0059 00:08:43 S2:   ·        One per cent a year for thirty years is a quarter of the final pot.
s0060 00:08:54 S1: ¶|·        A quarter seems far too large to be true.
s0061 00:09:00 S2: ¶|         Run the numbers and it is worse than that in a low return decade.
s0062 00:09:10 S2:            The fee is charged on the balance, so it grows exactly as your money grows.
s0063 00:09:20 S2:   ·        It is compound interest, working very patiently for somebody else.

s0067 00:09:56 S2:   ·        You cannot avoid the one without also missing the other.
